subject: Cognitive Science
title: Working Memory
description: A quick win: understand Working Memory.

hook.text: Hold a phone number in your head while finding a pen. That fragile juggling act is working memory.

buildup.text: Baddeley's model has four parts: a phonological loop, a visuospatial sketchpad, a buffer, and a boss.

discovery.text: The phonological loop repeats sounds. The sketchpad holds mental images. The central executive directs.

twist.text: Working memory capacity is tiny: about four chunks. Overload it and learning collapses.

climax.text: Individual differences in working memory predict reading skill, math ability, and fluid intelligence.

punchline.text: The size of your mental desk limits your thinking.

quiz.question: What is the capacity of working memory?

details.summary: Working memory is the mental workspace that holds and manipulates information in the moment. Baddeley's model includes a phonological loop for sounds, a visuospatial sketchpad for images, and a central executive that coordinates.
details.whyItMatters: Working memory capacity limits how much you can think about simultaneously. Understanding it explains cognitive bottlenecks in learning, problem-solving, and instruction design.
takeaways: Working memory holds roughly four items at a time
Baddeley's model includes verbal, visual, and executive components
Its capacity limits learning and problem-solving ability

faq.question: How does working memory differ from short-term memory?
faq.answer: Short-term memory simply holds information briefly. Working memory actively manipulates it. Solving a math problem in your head uses working memory because you must hold numbers and operate on them simultaneously. The active processing component is what distinguishes working memory.

faq.question: Can working memory capacity be increased?
faq.answer: Training on working memory tasks can improve performance on those specific tasks, but broader transfer to general intelligence is debated. More effective strategies include chunking, which groups information to fit within capacity limits, and offloading to external aids like notes and diagrams.
